package.description:
If you have severe stomach pain that will not go away, with or without nausea or vomiting, stop taking it and call your healthcare provider right away. For signs of a serious allergic reaction, call your emergency number or get medical help right away, and stop taking it. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.

Quick answer: Foundayo (orforglipron) is a once-daily GLP-1 pill. In the label's Trial 1 (adults without type 2 diabetes with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition), the top label dose gave an average 11.1% weight loss vs 2.1% on placebo at 72 weeks, alongside diet and activity. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were higher during dose escalation and decreased over time.

Sources:
1. US Prescribing Information, rev 7/2026: https://uspl.lilly.com/foundayo/foundayo.html?s=pi
2. Medication Guide, rev 7/2026: https://uspl.lilly.com/foundayo/foundayo.html?s=mg

Turned around, nearly 9 in 10 on that arm didn't stop for adverse events. Save this for your next appointment. Not personal advice. script.working_title: Orforglipron (Foundayo) Pill: What Should You Expect?
script.hook_pattern: A 'you' scenario folded into an answer-first opener (Exp H). Sentence 1 names orforglipron and gives a hedged answer: you may notice less appetite, and nausea, vomiting and diarrhea that were higher during dose increases. The label's headline number (top label dose -11.1% vs placebo -2.1%) is spoken by about 15 s. A second concrete payoff (one pill a day, with or without food) lands by about 28 s. A one-sentence open loop (how many people stopped because of adverse events) pays off in the 'Who actually stopped' chapter.

scenes.narration: If you're starting orforglipron, the Foundayo pill, you may notice less appetite, and nausea, vomiting and diarrhea that were higher during dose increases.
scenes.on_screen_text: Orforglipron (Foundayo): less appetite; nausea, vomiting, diarrhea higher during dose increases
scenes.retention_device: Answer-first hook: drug and hedged answer in sentence 1

scenes.narration: In the label's Trial One, in adults without type two diabetes, the highest label dose lowered weight more than placebo. The average loss was eleven point one percent of body weight, at seventy-two weeks. On placebo, it was two point one percent.
scenes.on_screen_text: Average weight loss: top label dose vs placebo

visual.stat_label: Top label dose -11.1% vs placebo -2.1%, adults with obesity or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without type 2 diabetes, 72 weeks

scenes.retention_device: Headline number by 15 s, with its placebo comparator

scenes.narration: In everyday life, that can start at dinner, when you push your plate away sooner than usual. And in the trials, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were higher during dose escalation and decreased over time.
scenes.retention_device: Lived moment folded into the answer

scenes.narration: Second thing to know: it's one pill a day, and the label says you can take it with or without food.
scenes.on_screen_text: Once a day, with or without food

scenes.narration: Later, I'll show you the one number that tells you how many people actually stopped because of adverse events.
scenes.retention_device: Open loop (pays off in 'Who actually stopped')

scenes.narration: Imagine Dana, fifty-two, at the pharmacy counter with her first pack. She's hopeful, a little nervous, and full of questions.

visual.stock_query: nervous hopeful woman at pharmacy counter

scenes.narration: We'll answer them from the label and the Medication Guide: how the pill works, what the trial found, and which signs mean call right away.
scenes.retention_device: Promise of what the viewer will get

scenes.narration: First, what this pill is actually doing inside you.
GLP-1 is a hormone your own gut releases after you eat. It helps signal fullness, helps release insulin when blood sugar rises, and slows how fast your stomach empties.
But your body's own GLP-1 is broken down within a couple of minutes. Orforglipron acts on the same receptor, and it lasts long enough for one pill a day.
Here's where it gets interesting. Semaglutide and tirzepatide are peptides, chains of amino acids, the kind of molecule digestion tends to break apart.
Orforglipron isn't a peptide. It's a small molecule, which is part of why it can come as a simple daily pill.
scenes.on_screen_text: A small molecule, not a peptide

scenes.narration: For Dana, the change may not feel dramatic. Maybe the afternoon snack she always reaches for just starts to feel optional.
If you've ever felt appetite was a willpower problem, you're not alone. The biology says it isn't only that.

visual.stock_query: relieved person, weight lifting off shoulders

scenes.narration: But a quieter appetite raises the big question. How much weight did people actually lose, and what does an average mean for you?
Let's unpack that eleven percent.

In the label's Trial One, adults without type two diabetes who had obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, lost more weight on the highest label dose than on placebo over seventy-two weeks.
scenes.on_screen_text: Obesity, or overweight plus weight-related condition
scenes.retention_device: Result and population in one sentence

scenes.narration: That was alongside a reduced-calorie diet and more activity, not instead of them. The average loss was eleven point one percent. On placebo, it was two point one percent.

visual.stat_label: Top label dose -11.1% vs placebo -2.1%, adults with obesity or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without type 2 diabetes, 72 weeks
visual.stock_query: pill next to vegetables and sneakers

scenes.retention_device: Number restated with context and comparator

scenes.narration: To feel that number, think of roughly one pound out of every nine you started with. That's our rough math, not a promise.
And an average hides a range. Some people lost more, some lost less, and no trial can tell you in advance which you'll be.

visual.stock_query: many different people on a spectrum

scenes.narration: You may also see eleven point two percent online. That's the journal paper's figure for the same trial's top-dose group, which it calls thirty-six milligrams. The approved tablet's top dose is seventeen point two milligrams.

visual.stat_label: Journal report: top dose (36 mg) -11.2% vs placebo -2.1%, adults without type 2 diabetes, 72 weeks

scenes.retention_device: Explains the other number you'll see online

scenes.narration: Weight is one health measure among many. Your prescriber looks at the whole picture, including how you feel day to day.
But here's what people really ask at the pharmacy counter. What will it feel like in my stomach?
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer before chapter change

scenes.narration: Side effects next, because knowing them takes some of the fear out.
The Medication Guide lists the most common side effects. The stomach ones are nausea, constipation, diarrhea, vomiting, indigestion, stomach pain, a swollen belly, belching, heartburn and gas.
The rest of that list is headache, feeling tired and hair loss.
Here's the reassuring part. In the trials, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were higher during dose escalation, and decreased over time.
Dose escalation means the planned step-ups your prescriber uses to reach your dose. That plan is theirs to set with you.
Imagine Dana the evening after a step-up. Dinner sits heavily, she feels queasy, and she wonders if something's wrong.

visual.stock_query: queasy woman at dinner table, dark night room

scenes.narration: That worry makes sense. It also fits the pattern the label describes: more nausea, vomiting and diarrhea during escalation, decreasing over time.
Simple habits can help with nausea: smaller, more frequent meals, going easy on fried or greasy food, and getting plenty of fresh air.

items: Easy on fried or greasy food

scenes.narration: Sip fluids through the day, unless you've been told to limit fluids. The label warns that losing fluid from vomiting or diarrhea can lead to kidney problems.
If nausea, or any side effect, is bothering you, tell your prescriber. There may be ways to make it easier, and you decide that together.
And if you spot more hair in your brush than usual, that can feel upsetting. It's on the list, and it's worth raising at your next visit.
So the side effects are real. But how many people actually stopped because of adverse events? Here's the number I promised.
scenes.retention_device: Sets up payoff of main open loop

scenes.narration: First, one quick definition that changes how you hear it.
Adverse events are anything unwanted that happens to someone in a trial, whether or not the drug caused it. A bad cold counts.

visual.stock_query: person with cold in trial clinic

scenes.narration: In the journal's report of that top-dose group, more people stopped because of adverse events than on placebo. It was ten point three percent.

visual.stat_label: Stopped for adverse events: top dose (journal, 36 mg) 10.3% vs placebo 2.7%, adults without type 2 diabetes, 72 weeks

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: On placebo, it was two point seven percent.
Turn that around, and nearly nine in ten people on that arm did not stop because of adverse events.
scenes.on_screen_text: Nearly 9 in 10 didn't stop for adverse events

scenes.narration: So stopping was more common than on a dummy pill. That's exactly why your prescriber wants to hear early if something bothers you.
Which brings us to what protects you most: what to tell your prescriber before your first pill.
Think of this as your pre-appointment sticky note.
Start with your history. Tell them if you or anyone in your family has ever had MTC, or if you have MEN 2. MTC is a rare thyroid cancer, and MEN 2 is a rare inherited condition.
scenes.on_screen_text: MTC in you or your family, or MEN 2

scenes.narration: Mention any past problems with your pancreas or kidneys, severe liver problems, severe stomach problems like slow stomach emptying, called gastroparesis, or a history of diabetic eye disease, called diabetic retinopathy.
Tell them if you're pregnant, planning a pregnancy, or breastfeeding.

Bring your full medicine list. Low blood sugar is more likely if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea, a type of diabetes pill. Low blood sugar has also been reported in adults without type two diabetes.
And before any surgery or procedure with anesthesia or deep sedation, tell every healthcare provider involved that you take it.
There's one more set of signs worth knowing. And oddly, knowing them is what lets you relax about the rest.
scenes.on_screen_text: Know these, relax about the rest

scenes.narration: These are the few signs that mean don't wait.
Severe stomach pain that won't go away, with or without nausea or vomiting, can be a sign of pancreatitis. The Medication Guide says to stop taking it and call your healthcare provider right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Severe stomach pain: call right away

visual.stock_query: person calling doctor, dark night kitchen

scenes.retention_device: Clear sign plus action in one line

scenes.narration: Pain in your upper stomach, fever, yellowing skin or eyes, or clay-colored stools can point to gallbladder problems. Tell your healthcare provider right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Gallbladder signs: tell them right away

scenes.narration: For signs of a serious allergic reaction, call your emergency number or get medical help right away, and stop taking it.
That means swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat; trouble breathing or swallowing; severe rash or itching; fainting or feeling dizzy; or a very rapid heartbeat.

items: Swelling of face, lips, tongue, throat

scenes.narration: An FDA drug safety communication also describes a potential risk of a rare eye condition called NAION with GLP-1 medicines, including orforglipron. If you suddenly lose vision or your vision changes, contact your healthcare provider right away.
scenes.on_screen_text: Potential NAION risk: sudden vision change

visual.stock_query: person covering one eye, calling doctor

scenes.retention_device: Last new fact, with action in the same line

scenes.narration: For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Talk it through with your prescriber.
scenes.on_screen_text: Don't stop or change on your own

scenes.narration: Here's the upside. Knowing these few signs means you don't have to treat every twinge as an emergency.
scenes.on_screen_text: Not every twinge is an emergency
scenes.retention_device: Pays off s49 paradox loop, ends chapter on relief

scenes.narration: So, back to Dana at the pharmacy counter, pack in hand.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card and return to thread

scenes.narration: What should she expect? Possibly less appetite, and nausea, vomiting and diarrhea that were higher during dose escalation and decreased over time.
scenes.on_screen_text: Possibly less appetite; GI effects higher during escalation, then decreased

visual.stock_query: storm cloud clearing over smiling woman

scenes.narration: On the highest label dose, in the label's Trial One, in adults without type two diabetes, the average weight loss was eleven point one percent. On placebo, it was two point one percent.

visual.stat_label: Top label dose -11.1% vs placebo -2.1%, adults with obesity or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without type 2 diabetes, 72 weeks

scenes.retention_device: Recap at exact number, with comparator

scenes.narration: And nearly nine in ten on the top dose didn't stop because of adverse events.
scenes.on_screen_text: Nearly 9 in 10 didn't stop for adverse events

scenes.narration: And if the pill turns out not to suit her, that isn't a personal failure. It's information she and her prescriber use together.
Picture her walking out of the pharmacy, pack in her bag, knowing what's normal, what to watch for, and who to call.
Here's your starting checklist. Three things, the same ones Dana takes with her.
scenes.on_screen_text: Three things to take with you

scenes.narration: One. Bring your own and your family's history and your full medicine list, written down, so nothing gets missed.
Two. Eat smaller meals, go easy on fried or greasy food, and sip fluids, unless you've been told to limit fluids.
Three. Know the call-right-away signs, so an everyday queasy evening doesn't have to scare you.
And bring your questions. Which step am I on? What should I do if eating gets hard? When will we check in?
If you've been hoping for something that feels doable, a once-daily pill is a real option to ask about. Your prescriber can tell you if it fits you.
scenes.on_screen_text: A real option to ask about

scenes.narration: Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether orforglipron is right for you.
If this made starting feel a little less mysterious, subscribe. We turn labels and trials into plain-English guides like this one, so your next appointment feels easier.

factcheck.summary: I checked the script's claims against the Foundayo prescribing information and Medication Guide (both revised 7/2026), the FDA's 9 Nov 2026 safety communication on NAION (a rare eye condition), the NHS nausea page (reviewed 17 Nov 2023), the federal definition of an adverse event (21 CFR 312.32) and the ATTAIN-1 trial results. The main numbers are correct. Trial 1 on the label: 11.1% weight loss on the top label dose vs 2.1% on placebo at 72 weeks. Journal report: 11.2% on 36 mg. Top label dose: 17.2 mg. The ACC summary confirms the -11.2% and -2.1% figures and stopping-for-adverse-events rates of about 5–10% vs 3%. The PubMed page wouldn't load, so I couldn't open the exact 10.3% vs 2.7%. Those figures match the rounded ACC rates and the channel's known Foundayo figures. Other checks that passed: the label's wording that nausea, vomiting and diarrhea were higher during dose escalation and decreased over time; the most-common side effect list; the pancreatitis, gallbladder and allergy signs; the dehydration-to-kidney warning; low blood sugar in adults without type 2 diabetes; surgery disclosure; the "potential" NAION wording; the NHS nausea tips; and the adverse-event definition. The safety lines are present: the emergency triggers come first, the scoped don't-stop line follows them, and the prescriber line is in place. The 1-in-9 pounds arithmetic is labelled as our own math. The Dana scenes are clearly hypothetical. I found only small wording and scope fixes, listed below.

thumbnail.reasoning:
All three are clean, high-contrast, single-focal-point designs with legible text at phone size (bold headline over a dark/saturated background, white subtext bar naming the drug). None give the answer away, none have a text/emotion mismatch, and none repeat the title's exact wording.

#0 "FIRST PILL NERVES?" pairs a worried, sweating pill character with a question that directly mirrors the viewer's likely emotional state when starting Foundayo, which is exactly what the title promises ("what to expect when you start"). The face's nervous expression matches the nervous headline, the curiosity gap (what actually happens) is open, and the subtext clearly names the drug. This is the tightest match between packaging and content and has the strongest emotional hook.

#1 "1 IN 10" is a strong curiosity device (a bare stat creates a question: who, why) and the worried stomach character's expression matches the tension of "stopped in trial," but the angle (dropout/adverse events) is a narrower slice of a broader "what to expect when starting" video, so it may slightly overpromise a different angle than the title centers on.

#2 "WHAT CHANGES FIRST?" is pure mystery via a silhouette pill and question mark, but it lacks any face or expressive character, so it has less emotional pull than the other two even though it's perfectly legible and directly on-topic.

Given equal legibility, #0 wins on CTR because it combines curiosity with the strongest emotional anchor (a relatable worried expression) tied most directly to the video's stated promise.</reasoning>
